# RFC 4506 reference audit results
## Audit scope
Every `RFC 4506 §X` (and bare `RFC 4506`) citation in the repository was located via `grep -rn "RFC 4506\|RFC4506\|rfc4506\|rfc 4506"` across `Sources/`, `Tests/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, and `README.ko.md`, then cross-checked against the actual section numbers and section bodies of `docs/rfc4506.txt`.
Real top-level structure of RFC 4506 (XDR: External Data Representation Standard):
- §1 Introduction - §2 Changes from RFC 1832 - §3 Basic Block Size - §4 XDR Data Types - §4.1 Integer - §4.2 Unsigned Integer - §4.3 Enumeration - §4.4 Boolean - §4.5 Hyper Integer and Unsigned Hyper Integer - §4.6 Floating-Point - §4.7 Double-Precision Floating-Point - §4.8 Quadruple-Precision Floating-Point - §4.9 Fixed-Length Opaque Data - §4.10 Variable-Length Opaque Data - §4.11 String - §4.12 Fixed-Length Array - §4.13 Variable-Length Array - §4.14 Structure - §4.15 Discriminated Union - §4.16 Void - §4.17 Constant - §4.18 Typedef - §4.19 Optional-Data - §4.20 Areas for Future Enhancement - §5 Discussion - §6 The XDR Language Specification - §7 An Example of an XDR Data Description - §8 Security Considerations - §9 IANA Considerations - §10 Trademarks and Owners - §11 ANSI/IEEE Standard 754-1985
## Result: 0 hallucinations
All RFC 4506 citations in the repository were verified to point at the section that actually defines the cited content. No edits were made.

## FYI: RFC 4506 §4.11 wording vs nanonfs `writeString`
The doc comment at `XDR.swift:117` describes XDR strings as a "variable-length opaque of **UTF-8** bytes". RFC 4506 §4.11 itself says "**ASCII** bytes":
> The standard defines a string of n (numbered 0 through > n-1) ASCII bytes to be the number n encoded as an > unsigned integer ...
This is not a hallucinated section number — §4.11 *is* String, and the structural encoding (length-prefixed, 4-byte padded) described in the comment is exactly what §4.11 mandates. The UTF-8 part comes from the application protocol layered on top: NFSv4 (RFC 7530 §1.4.3 "Internationalization") explicitly mandates UTF-8 for `utf8string` / `component4` / `linktext4` and friends. The nanonfs comment is therefore describing the composition (RFC 4506 §4.11 framing + NFSv4 UTF-8 content) rather than a verbatim quote of §4.11. Left as-is, since the section reference is correct and the practical encoding described matches how nanonfs is actually used. Flagging only in case the maintainer wants to tighten the wording later (e.g. "§4.11 — string framing; NFSv4 mandates UTF-8 content").
## Build status
No code changes were made by this audit, so build / test status is unchanged from before the audit.
agent-task-report.note:
# Audit method note
- Driven entirely by `grep` over the working tree plus direct reads of `docs/rfc4506.txt`. No memory-based reasoning about RFC 4506 section numbers was used (per `CLAUDE.md` §4 anti-hallucination rule, generalized to RFC 4506 / 5531 in the same spirit). - Outcome contrasts notably with the same day's RFC 7530 (many defects) and RFC 5531 (3 defects) audits. RFC 4506 has a shallow, stable, well-cited section structure (§4.1..§4.20 for data types, with no contested numbering between RFC 4506 and the older RFC 1832), so the failure modes that bit the 7530/5531 audits — op-number-vs-§16 offset, hallucinated appendix sub-numbers — simply have no analogue here. Worth recording so future agents do not waste cycles re-auditing this surface.
